title: MolEmb: Multimodal Large Language Models Can Be Strong Molecular Embedding Models
abstract: Molecular embedding models can serve as foundational infrastructure for computational chemistry and drug discovery, where reusable vector representations support property prediction, virtual screening, and retrieval. Most molecular encoders are specialist models built around a single molecular view, producing unconditional vectors with no language interface for varying the representation. We ask whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which natively process images, text, and symbolic inputs, can instead serve as \emph{general molecular embedding models} that produce embeddings conditioned on both a molecular profile and a natural-language semantic context. We introduce \textbf{MolEmb}, a lightweight framework that adapts MLLMs by aligning molecular profiles with textual descriptions in a shared embedding space using a bidirectional contrastive objective. The resulting embedding model is competitive on molecular property prediction and supports cross-modal molecule--text retrieval in the same space. We further introduce \textbf{MolCAR}, a diagnostic benchmark for context-aware retrieval, and find that context-aware molecular embedding is primarily a data property of the supervision. These results suggest that MLLMs are not merely chemistry assistants or generators, but a viable and extensible route to general molecular embedding models.

title: Hit-Triage Pretrained Transformer (Hit-TPT), an Interaction-Agnostic Graph-Transformer for Post-docking Enrichment
abstract: Computational docking-based virtual screening is widely used to identify hit compounds in earlystage drug discovery. However, current docking methods still suffer from high false-positive rates, often resulting in no hits identified in campaigns against novel targets. For instance, in the first several CACHE challenges, the hit rate was consistently below 1%. This underscores the need for more selective and reliable triage methods. Here we present the Hit-Triage Pretrained Transformer (Hit-TPT), a graph neural network operating on protein-ligand interaction graphs to recognize true protein binders from decoys. Rooted in molecular recognition, Hit-TPT treats molecular complexes as 3D physical entities. It utilizes an interaction-agnostic graph transformer architecture combined with physics-informed atom features to reflect underlying chemical relationships while employing a novel 3D-positional encodings to represents the geometric context of each atom. The model was developed and evaluated using the DUD-E dataset, which comprises 102 targets with known actives and property matched decoys. To ensure rigorous validation, the model was trained on 77 targets and evaluated on a strictly held out test set of the remaining 25 targets. Hit-TPT achieved a mean Enrichment Factor in the top 1% of best-ranked ligands (EF1%) of 42 across these 25 test targets, substantially outperforming benchmarked conventional and ML-based methods. Crucially, we demonstrated that this high performance is not a dataset related artifact. Many previous machine learning models inadvertently function as ligand-only classifiers because training datasets rarely feature the same ligand across multiple targets with varying affinities. To prove Hit-TPT overcomes this limitation and learns genuine intermolecular interaction patterns rather than memorizing ligand scaffolds, we conducted a cross-target prediction analysis. This showed that Hit-TPT assigns high binding-probability scores to an active ligand exclusively when evaluated against its native target, confirming that the network successfully avoids ligand bias. Our results demonstrate that this physics-oriented architecture can markedly reduce false positives in virtual screening, offering a practical and generalizable approach to improve hit-finding efficiency by prioritizing compounds with genuine, target specific activity.

title: Fragment-Based Virtual Screening and Experimental Validation of MMP-9 Hemopexinlike Domain Inhibitors
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) is a key mediator of extracellular matrix remodeling and cancer metastasis, yet the development of selective inhibitors remains challenging due to high conservation of its catalytic domain. Targeting the less conserved hemopexin-like (PEX) domain offers a promising strategy for isoform-selective inhibition. Here, we report an integrated fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD) approach combining pharmacophore modelling, structure-based virtual screening, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and extensive biological validation to identify novel MMP-9 PEX domain inhibitors. Fragment screening and structure-guided optimization led to a focused series of indole-based derivatives, which exhibited favourable binding energies and stable interactions within the PEX domain, confirmed through MD simulations (n=3). The top candidates were synthesized and subjected to comprehensive biological evaluation, including cytotoxicity profiling across multiple cancer cell lines, colony formation, cell migration, apoptosis induction, mitochondrial membrane depolarization and flow-cytometric analysis. Among them, IN-06 demonstrated potent and selective antiproliferative activity against HCT-116 colon cancer cells while sparing noncancerous cells. Target-specific studies using immunofluorescence, gelatin zymography and enzyme-based fluorometric assays established that IN-06 effectively suppresses MMP-9 expression and enzymatic activity in a concentration-dependent manner. Overall, this work highlights the effectiveness of integrated computational modelling, synthesis and experimental validation for the discovery of novel MMP-9 PEX domain inhibitors and provides a promising chemical scaffold for further preclinical development.

title: A General-Purpose Molecular Foundation Model Transfers Across Diverse Olfactory Tasks
abstract: Foundation models have transformed molecular property prediction, yet it remains unclear whether a molecular foundation model, fine-tuned on a single canonical olfactory prediction task, can learn representations that transfer across diverse machine olfaction problems. We investigate this question by fine-tuning Uni-Mol2 on the GS-LF benchmark for multi-label odor descriptor prediction and evaluating the resulting model, without additional deep-learning training, on four complementary downstream settings: cross-dataset odor descriptor prediction, odorous-versus-odorless classification, enantiomer evaluation, and odor mixture discriminability. The fine-tuned model matches or exceeds the performance of the state-of-the-art olfaction-specific baseline on the primary GS-LF benchmark and consistently transfers across these downstream evaluations. The enantiomer analysis further shows that three-dimensional molecular representations distinguish mirror-image molecules in a way that two-dimensional graph models fundamentally cannot, although accurately predicting the perceptual consequences of stereochemistry remains an open challenge. Together, these results support a train-once, transfer-across-tasks paradigm for machine olfaction and suggest that chemically pretrained molecular representations provide a strong foundation for transferable olfactory prediction.

title: External Evaluation of Multi-Agent AI Systems in Drug Discovery: A PRISMA-Informed Scoping Review of the External-Evaluation Gap
abstract: Multi-agent large-language-model (LLM) systems are increasingly proposed for tasks across drug discovery and development. This PRISMA-informed scoping review examines a narrower question than capability surveys: whether reported system performance has been evaluated by investigators independent of the original developers. The review applies an explicit operational definition of multi-agent architecture and maps included systems to one of six stages: target identification, molecular screening, molecular design, lead optimization, delivery formulation, or clinical-trial workflows. Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) properties appear as an optimization objective within molecular design rather than as a separate stage, because no system in the corpus treats ADMET evaluation as its primary reported task. The curated primary corpus contains 13 unique systems satisfying the strict multi-agent definition. One system (STELLA) has an independent external evaluation, reported by an unaffiliated group through BioML-bench. Three systems (Robin, OriGene, LipoAgent) report author-run empirical validation in biological systems. One system (MT-Mol) reports author-run evaluation on third-party benchmarks. The remaining eight report author-curated computational evaluation only. Six benchmark resources are inventoried separately; four have no located deployment against any system in the corpus, and of the two that do, only one was run by an unaffiliated group. A pre-specified sensitivity analysis shows that the two additional systems with documented independent external evaluation — TrialGPT and Biomni — both fall outside the strict multi-agent boundary, indicating that independent evaluation currently concentrates in single-agent, modular, and general-purpose systems rather than in strict multiagent architectures. The review provides a transparent taxonomy, an explicit classification protocol with a stated precedence rule, and a versioned evidence ledger.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Antifungal Drug Discovery Against WHO Critical-Priority Pathogens: Toward a WHO-Aligned, Selectivity-Integrated Discovery Pipeline
abstract: Artificial intelligence has demonstrated real power in medicinal chemistry generally, yet it remains almost entirely absent from actual antifungal drug development, a gap made more urgent by rising antifungal resistance and a drug pipeline that has produced almost no genuinely new chemical classes in two decades. Invasive fungal infections, rising antifungal resistance, and a critically depleted drug pipeline together constitute a public health emergency that recent burden estimates suggest rivals tuberculosis in annual mortality. Since 2022, the WHO Fungal Priority Pathogen List has offered a strategic plan for prioritizing resources; however, the use of artificial intelligence in the discovery of antifungals is still scattered, and even the most recent and extensive scoping review of the literature (106 primary studies) outlined existing applications but did not suggest how to unify them. This review concludes that the gap must be addressed by shifting the focus of antifungal AI research from two concepts to two principles: pathogen prioritization that is directly taken from the WHO list, and therapeutic selectivity that is considered a scored, quantitative constraint that is applied at every pipeline stage instead of as an afterthought when potential compounds are already identified. We are proposing a conceptual pipeline with 6 steps: pathogen stratification, AI-enabled target validation, generative molecular design, multi-objective optimization, forward ADMET and resistance predictions, and experimental prioritization. We operationalize this with two tools: a scored Priority-Selectivity Matrix, demonstrated here with a worked numerical example across five real antifungal targets, and a Stage-Specific AI Toolkit. We further provide a critical appraisal of the specific published tools that already exist in this space, HitList, Fung-AI, FungAMR, and a 2026 pooled CRISPRi screen, showing precisely where each stops short of an integrated, selectivity-first system, and we identify a structural blind spot largely absent from prior antifungal AI literature: the highest-value antifungal targets are integral membrane proteins, the exact protein class that current structure-prediction and docking models handle least reliably. Finally, we remark that all the antifungal agents developed in the last five years have been developed by traditional medicinal chemistry, not AI, so the regulatory process for an AI-generated antifungal has never been tested. This synthesis is designed to translate the scene of a series of disconnected computational demonstrations to a prioritized, discovery-focused, quantitatively assessed effort in the realm of antifungals.

title: Mol-JEPA: A multimodal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Molecules
abstract: Despite recent advances in molecular foundation models, several limitations remain, such as chemically invalid augmentations, modality collapse, and incomplete representation of biochemical environments. To address these challenges, we present \textbf{Mol-JEPA}, a scalable framework for learning molecular world models. Rather than relying on suboptimal molecular perturbations, our model uses modality masking to exploit information from molecular structures, cellular phenotypes, binding affinities, ADMET profiles, quantum chemistry simulations and other drug discovery data. Across various benchmarks, we show that the representations learned by Mol-JEPA deliver strong performance, demonstrating the value of incorporating biochemical context through latent space prediction.

title: Cross-mixture-size graph neural network for CO2 solubility prediction in multicomponent amine solvents
abstract: Accurate prediction of equilibrium CO 2 loading in aqueous amine blends is essential for the design and screening of next-generation carbon capture solvents. However, existing machine learning models are generally developed for a fixed number of mixture components, limiting their applicability to increasingly complex solvent formulations. In this work, we introduced a mixture-size-invariant graph neural network (MSI-GNN) that enables prediction of CO 2 loading across different amine blend complexities within a single architecture. The model represents each amine-water-CO 2 system as a disjoint-union of graph, generates component-level representations using shared message-passing neural network, and combines solvent contributions through a learnable mole-fraction-weighted mixing rule. The resulting mixture context is integrated with CO 2 modulator and temperature descriptors to predict CO 2 equilibrium loading. Trained on 6,835 experimental data points spanning 121 solvent combinations, MSI-GNN achieves an R 2 of 0.987 ± 0.001 on the held-out test set and gives an R 2 of 0.913 ± 0.006 on the held-out test set aggregated from single-, dual-, and triple-amines. This demonstrates generalization beyond both the chemical systems and mixture complexities represented during model development. Benchmarking against a baseline GNN and its physics-informed variant demonstrates competitive accuracy on single-amine systems, while MSI-GNN uniquely extends prediction to binary and ternary blends without architectural modification. The mixture-size invariance provides a scalable approach for predicting previously unexplored multicomponent solvents and establishes a computational framework for accelerating high-throughput screening and discovery of next-generation amine-based CO 2 capture solvents.

title: Binding Affinity between Polymer Dots (Pdots) and Ovalbumin Protein at Varying pH
abstract: Determining the binding mechanisms between polymer dots and proteins is important for developing novel nanotechnologies for biomedicine and bioimaging. In this work, we use all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to determine the binding affinity of Pdots with ovalbumin protein at pH = 7 and 1. The selected Pdots are mixtures of Poly[(9,9-dioctylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl)-alt-co-(1,4-benzo-(2,1',3)-thiadiazole)] (PFBT) and poly(styrene/maleic anhydride) (PSMA) with varying composition. At pH = 7, the Pdots have a net negative charge due to the COO- functional groups on the PFBT, and the protein also has a net negative charge. At pH = 1, the Pdots are charge neutral with PFBT containing only COOH functional groups, and the protein also has a net positive charge. We sample the initial position of the protein by varying its initial position through all 6 orientations of a cube. For each orientation, we pull the protein towards the PFBT region of the Pdot. We compare the Coulombic and Lennard-Jones interaction energies for the 6 different interacting faces and two selected pH values. We find that the LJ interaction energies are similar among all 12 of these cases. The measured Coulombic interaction energies suggest that pH = 1 has better binding affinity than pH = 7. The potentials of mean force (PMF) along the pulling coordinates differ with pH. The PMFs from 2 of the 6 initial configurations at pH = 1 are negative whereas none of them are negative at pH = 7, confirming the preferred binding affinity when pH = 1. One of the faces at pH = 1 has the lowest PMF of about -30 kcal/mol, which is much lower than about 6 kcal/mol seen for the lowest case at pH = 7. Comparison of protein residue charge distributions at pH = 7 and 1 further shows that the electrostatic interaction is critical to the binding affinity, and negatively charged residues reduce at pH = 7 does not bind to negatively charged Pdot.

title: Real-time NMR analysis of glutamine metabolism for screening anti-cancer agents in living cells.
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming is a substantial obstacle for anticancer drug screening, as targeted therapeutics often lose efficiency due to the dynamic adaption of cancer cells. Glutamine metabolism in cancer profoundly impacts tumor initiation, progression and metastasis. The existing agents are compromised by resistance and off-target toxicity. In this study, a real-time NMR tracking method for intracellular glutamine metabolic flux was established. This method enables comprehensive profiling of nitrogen metabolism and serves as a valuable tool for characterizing specific cancer metabolic phenotypes and screening drugs against targeted cancer cells. Applying this approach to traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) discovery, we identified Astragalus membranaceus as a potent regulator of glutamine metabolism. Through virtual screening via molecular docking, 12 potential compounds from Astragalus membranaceus were initially flagged as candidate binders toward the allosteric pocket of glutaminase 1 (GLS1). Crucially, subsequent in vitro recombinant human GLS1 enzyme activity assays successfully ruled out computational false positives and demonstrated that Compound 2 (quercetin) acts as the exclusive, direct enzymatic inhibitor among the tested monomers, capable of effectively suppressing GLS1 activity. Overall, this work provides a robust platform for real-time metabolic profiling of glutamine metabolism and drug screening at the living cell level, and offers new insights into the mechanisms of TCMs in anticancer therapy.

title: DNA Directed Chemistry: Scalable Programmed DNA-Encoded Library Synthesis for More Chemically Diverse and Drug-Like Libraries
abstract: DNA-Encoded Libraries (DELs) are indispensable high-throughput platforms in drug discovery, but the widely adopted split-and-pool synthesis method is fundamentally limited: the DNA merely records, rather than directs, the steps of chemistry. This lack of programmatic control imposes mandatory downstream chemistry congruency, restricts structural diversity, and inevitably generates a combinatorial explosion of un-drug-like molecules, hindering both hit-finding and the acquisition of structurally informative data required for machine learning (ML) models. To resolve these core constraints, we developed Programmed DEL Synthesis (PDS), a robust, industrially applicable platform for non-combinatorial DEL construction in which the DNA actively directs the synthesis. PDS is built upon a sort-and-pool mechanism expanded by three key innovations: sequence-specific installation of first building blocks using charged carrier codons, a multinomial encoding strategy that enables libraries exceeding 20 billion unique encodings in three chemical steps, and non-combinatorial germline assembly that allows for the programmatic omission of undesirable building block combinations. We demonstrate the platform with Library i01, a three-step, threepathway library employing 137 trifunctional scaffolds. The design successfully programmed the systematic merging and un-merging of three mutually incompatible reaction pathways: Acid→Aldehyde→Amine, Amine→Aldehyde→Acid, and Aldehyde→Acid→Amine within a single synthesis. Pilot affinity selections against Carbonic Anhydrase (BCA-II) validated the high fidelity of DNA encoding and efficient building block installation across all steps and pathways, confirming the platform's robust utility for selection. PDS transforms chemical congruency and drug-likeness into programmable properties, offering a precise, efficient solution that improves library quality without sacrificing chemical space. Crucially, PDS enables the construction of structurally tailored 2nd Generation DELs needed to provide the high-resolution data required for productive ML-driven active learning cycles, establishing a critical operational link for modern drug development.

title: Bridging Food Chemistry and Computational Approaches with Agentic AI: Plant Protein Solubility and Bioactive-Enzyme Interactions
abstract: Computational approaches can provide valuable molecular-level and data-driven insights for food chemistry research, but their broader use remains limited by the need for specialized computational and programming expertise. In this study, we propose a human–AI collaborative framework that bridges food chemistry and computational approaches through simple, visible, step-by-step agentic AI workflow design. The framework enables food scientists to translate domain-specific hypotheses into computational workflows that can be planned, implemented, tested, refined, and reused with AI assistance. Two practical applications are presented. The first uses surface-based structural descriptors to investigate plant protein water solubility. Principal component analysis explained 94.19% of the total variance in the first two components and distinguished proteins with greater surface exposure of charged residues from those enriched in surface-exposed Asn/Gln or nonpolar residues, which may favor protein–protein interactions and lower water solubility. The second integrates AlphaFold 3-based structural prediction and MM/GBSA binding affinity estimation to investigate interactions between food-derived polyphenols and pancreatic lipase. The predicted binding-affinity ranking of quercetin > curcumin > resveratrol was consistent with reported enzymatic inhibition trends, while residue-level analysis suggested that hydrophobic contacts and interactions with catalytic residues, particularly Ser153, contribute to ligand stabilization near the catalytic region. Together, these examples demonstrate how food chemistry hypotheses can be translated into clear, traceable, and reusable agentic AI workflows, lowering technical barriers to computational food chemistry while supporting both task execution and computational learning.

title: Docking-Score Landscapes Shape Active-Learning Performance across Vina, Glide, and SILCS
abstract: The rapid expansion of large chemical libraries has created a need for virtual screening workflows that are both efficient and accurate. Active learning (AL) offers a scalable strategy by iteratively training surrogate models to prioritize promising compounds and reduce the number of required docking calculations. However, direct benchmarking of active-learning protocols across docking engines remains limited. In this study, we ask whether docking scores generated by different docking engines affect AL performance and what factors underlie these differences. To do so, we compare four active-learning virtual screening workflows, Vina-MolPAL, Glide-MolPAL, SILCS-MolPAL, and Schrödinger’s active-learning Glide, across multiple protein targets and library sizes. Performance was assessed by recovery of top-scoring molecules according to each workflow’s respective docking engine, score-prediction accuracy, chemical diversity, and computational cost. Vina-MolPAL achieved the highest top-1% recovery at a 1% batch size, whereas SILCS-MolPAL achieved comparable recovery at a larger batch size. Latent-embedding analyses suggest that the docking-score landscape strongly influences active-learning performance. In addition, combining active learning with SILCS provides a computationally efficient, membrane-aware approach for screening compounds at transmembrane binding sites.

title: Vector-Guided Drug Action via Active-Site Electric Fields: A Theoretical Framework Combining Quantum-Mechanical/Molecular-Mechanical Modeling and Vibrational Stark Tuning Principles
abstract: Traditional rational drug design paradigms rely primarily on spatial complementary interactionssteric fit, localized hydrogen-bonding topologies, and static lipophilicity profiles—within macromolecular binding pockets. These models largely omit the catalytic and kinetic contributions of the large-scale, oriented endogenous electrostatic fields generated within structured enzymatic and receptor microenvironments. Building on experimentally established vibrational Stark effect (VSE) spectroscopy of enzyme active sites, we present a theoretical framework for Vector-Guided Pharmacology, in which the directional alignment between a pharmacophore’s transition dipole moment (∆µ ‡) or ground-state dipole (µ g) and the intrinsic active-site electric field vector (Epocket) is proposed as a determinant of binding affinity and the activation free-energy barrier (∆G‡) for covalent and non-covalent ligand stabilization. We formulate an electrostatic-embedding QM/MM Hamiltonian, consistent with polarizablemultipole (AMOEBA-type) force-field architectures, and derive the linear and quadratic Stark perturbation terms that couple a ligand’s dipole and polarizability to Epocket. Using representative, literature-consistent parameter values (field magnitudes of 10–50 MV/cm, as established by VSE spectroscopy, and transition dipole differences of several debye, typical of polarizable electrophilic warheads), we present illustrative worked evaluations of the model showing that parallel vector alignment can, in principle, lower the activation free energy by several kcal/mol relative to the antialigned configuration. These worked examples are direct, reproducible evaluations of the derived equations for assumed input parameters; they are not the output of new density-functional-theory (DFT) or molecular-dynamics (MD) calculations performed for this study, and no such calculations are claimed. The framework is offered as a conceptual and mathematical foundation, together with a proposed computational validation protocol, for treating electrostatic vector alignment as an orthogonal, testable parameter in rational drug design.

title: Virtual screening of approved drugs nominates tofogliflozin for the SHP2 allosteric pocket
abstract: SHP2 supports oncogenic RAS–MAPK signaling, and ligands in its regulatory allosteric pocket can stabilize the autoinhibited state. Approved drugs were screened for an accessible probe of this pocket. A combined ranking of docking scores and interaction fidelity to the crystallographic SHP099 contact pattern prioritized compounds for simulation. In a matched benchmark of target-level SHP2 actives and property-matched decoys, the ranking achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.892 and 21.42-fold enrichment in the top 2% of the list. Short molecular dynamics simulations and comparative MM/GBSA narrowed the candidates, and successive 100 ns simulations reduced them to tofogliflozin. Across three independently seeded trajectories, mean ligand center-of-mass drift was 1.407–2.091 Å. Reference-matched hydrophobic contacts occurred in 97.3–100.0% of frames, and hydrogen bonds matching the reference pattern occurred in 34.0–86.2%. Three absolute binding free-energy protocol repeats from one shared coordinate model gave ∆G = −10.33 kcal mol −1 with a reported uncertainty of 0.53 kcal mol −1 , supporting numerical repeatability within that model. Experimental measurements of binding and pocket dependence, followed by SHP2 activity assays, are needed to confirm the proposed interaction and determine whether it produces inhibition.

title: Differential Learning for Robust Prediction of Thermal Stability with Application to Energetic Materials
abstract: Predicting thermal stability during handling and storage is essential for the design of safe and reliable energetic materials. However, experimental measurements vary significantly across laboratories due to differences in protocols and analysis methods, making it difficult to train reliable predictive models. We address this challenge through differential learning. Rather than predicting absolute decomposition temperatures, we instead train message passing neural networks to predict relative differences between pairs of molecules. This approach reduces sensitivity to systematic experimental errors and achieves >85% accuracy in ranking compounds by thermal stability, outperforming conventional regression methods on the same heterogeneous dataset. To understand what drives these predictions, we compare neural network models with interpretable alternatives built from descriptors derived from ab initio calculations and cheminformatics software. This analysis identifies bond dissociation enthalpy as a key determinant of thermal stability rankings, providing further insight into the complex chemistry of thermal decomposition. The differential learning framework generalizes across model architectures, from graph neural networks to classical descriptor-based approaches. Our results demonstrate that learning relative properties rather than absolute values offers a practical solution for modeling noisy experimental data, with direct applications in materials design where thermal stability predictions inform safety protocols.

title: What Cycle Closure Can and Cannot See in a Relative Binding Free Energy Network
abstract: Cycle closure is the standard consistency check on a perturbation network, and what such a check can see is fixed by the gradient–cycle decomposition of edge flows (HodgeRank): the cycle part of a network’s error is auditable and biases nothing, while the gradient part biases the affinities and is invisible to any statistic computed from the network’s own values, at any magnitude. Both parts are measured here on 1145 real binding edges. The auditable subspace spans a third of the error space and, in the variance-weighted metric the closure statistic uses, carries under one per cent of the error against experiment. Experimental and annotation error is per-ligand, so it falls in the invisible part by construction and can only have made that share smaller: the measurement is a floor, and it survives correction: in the metric the closure statistic uses on every system measured, at one cell as a tie, and in an isotropic reading on every system of the wider grounded set, failing only on the two weakest of the four the test itself selected. The test built on it behaves as the bound predicts, and its flag set is not stable: the per-edge residuals and the ranking of systems reproduce across independent repeats, and the list of flagged systems does not. Fitting closure against the precisions the estimator already reports gives that test its stated null; it ties the standard fixed 1.0 kcal/mol cutoff, and on every replicate the set of systems it flags lies inside the set that cutoff flags. It flags nothing once the reported errors are widened by half, enough to cover the pose and preparation variance the protocol repeats hold fixed, and it names no removal that recovers accuracy against experiment. Resolving the gradient part needs measurements from outside the network, at worst one per unresolved dimension.

title: Gromov-Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation
abstract: Graphs are invariant under node permutations, motivating the use of permutation-equivariant architectures in generative models. In flow matching, however, symmetry may also enter the source--target coupling: once graph pairs are compared up to node relabeling, the natural Wasserstein geometry is that of the graph quotient space. The Euclidean quotient metric of this space coincides with the Gromov--Monge distance, obtained by optimally relabeling the nodes. We develop this perspective theoretically, showing that quotient couplings can be lifted to aligned representatives without additional cost and that symmetrization yields equivariant flow-matching minimizers, including for categorical endpoint prediction. In practice, exact Gromov--Monge alignment is intractable, so we construct minibatch couplings using efficient Gromov--Wasserstein-type relaxations and lower bounds for the inner node alignment, optionally combined with an outer assignment between graphs. The resulting procedure changes only the training coupling and is compatible with standard permutation-equivariant architectures. Across continuous graph and categorical molecular generation, these structure-aware couplings substantially improve sample quality at small integration budgets, while our scaled-up molecular models remain competitive under conventional many-step sampling.

title: Site-Resolved Prediction of Mayr Nucleophilicity with Reactivity-Pretrained Graph Neural Networks
abstract: The magnitude of a compound’s nucleophilicity is pivotal to mechanistic studies and rational catalyst design. Over the past decades, Mayr and co-workers developed an invaluable framework for quantifying nucleophilicity, comprising N parameters. Nevertheless, achieving accurate nucleophilic site prediction and low-cost quantification remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we construct a nucleophilicity prediction model, termed PPGNS (Pretrained and Physicochemical feature–augmented Graph neural network model for joint Nucleophilicity and Site prediction). By integrating carefully designed physicochemical and physical organic descriptors and extended tight-binding (xTB) calculations, graph neural networks (GNN) are employed to predict the N parameters, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) adopted for mechanistic interpretation. The PPGNS model achieves a higher accuracy and efficiency performance for N prediction relative to previous benchmark studies, with R 2 of 0.94 and 0.95 for automatic-site and known-site evaluations, both from pooled (out of fold) OOF predictions across five outer folds. Most notably, PPGNS enables site-resolved nucleophilicity prediction, achieving 93% Top-1 and 98% Top-3 recovery of nucleophilic reaction sites, a capability not reported in previous studies.

title: XGBoost Prediction of Ionizable Lipid Transfection Potency with Chemistry-Aware Validation
abstract: Ionizable lipids play key determinant role for the mRNA delivery performance of lipid nanoparticles (LNP), yet structure-activity relationships (SAR) for this compound class remain difficult to generalize across chemically diverse head groups and tail architectures. We used the publicly available AGILE ionizable lipid library, 1200 lipids synthesized by three-component Ugi reaction chemistry and formulated into LNPs carrying firefly luciferase reporter mRNA, to build an interpretable quantitative structure-transfection model based on extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFP4), four physiochemical descriptors, and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost). Because random data splitting inflates apparent predictive performance for structurally similar compound libraries, we designed a distance-buffered leave-one-cluster-out (LOCO) validation protocol that excludes any training compound within a Tanimoto distance of 0.1 from a held-out cluster, verified to eliminate chemical neighbor leakage. Under random five-fold cross validation, the model explained 48.9% of transfection variance (pooled R2 = 0.489, RMSE = 2.31), while under the buffered LOCO protocol measuring extrapolation to structurally novel chemotypes, pooled R2 fell to 0.354 (RMSE = 2.64, n = 938 of 1200 compound covered). This gap is real but moderate, and narrower than a naive per-cluster averaging of the same predictions would suggest. SHAP analysis, aggregated across all 50 LOCO folds to assess both stability and direction identified a head-group-ring-dependent instead of amine-presence-dependent structure-activity relationship: a piperazine head group was the single most stable determinant of predicted transfection potency and was consistently associated with reduced potency, while a cis-alkene tail motif showed a direction dependent on its position along the acyl tail, confirmed at both the individual-fold and pooled-split level. Calculated logP showed a moderate, mostly consistent, positive association with predicted potency. Molecular weight contributed comparable magnitude but a directionally inconsistent, collinearity confounded signal. This substructure-level finding converges independently with the original AGILE study, which used a mechanistically unrelated approach (integrated gradients on a graph neural network fit to Mordred descriptors) and identified a tertiary-amine descriptor (SssNH) as similarly influential for the same HeLa cell endpoint. We also integrate a nearest-neighbor applicability domain check into the prediction workflow so that candidate lipids structurally distant from the training library are flagged. We discuss the scope limitations of the underlying dataset, in particular its dependence on a single reporter mRNA and a single cell line, and position chemistry-aware generalization testing as a validation practice that should accompany in vitro confirmation of computationally prioritized ionizable lipid.

title: Beyond the Magic Methyl Effect: Activity Cliff Asymmetry of Functional Group Substitution in Drug Discovery
abstract: Activity cliffs occur in drug discovery programmes when a small structural change leads to a very large change in biological activity. We have used a matched molecular pair approach for common functional groups to establish examples of activity cliffs. We then measure how positive and negative activity cliffs are over-represented relative to a normal distribution. The ‘Magic Methyl Effect’ highlighted examples of where methylation led to significant activity increases, yet our data suggests that negative activity cliffs are more common than positive ones for methyl, and that significant increases are less common than most other functional groups. We show that both scaffold and substitution position effects play an important role in the occurrence of activity cliffs.

title: Binding mechanism of the DOPA-deficient mussel foot protein dbfp7 on rutile TiO2(110): an all-atom molecular dynamics study.
abstract: Protein adhesion to titanium dioxide surface underlies both biological implants and mussel based wet adhesives and is commonly attributed to the post translationally modified catechol bearing wild amino acid 2,3-dihydroxyphenylalanine. However, how the DOPA deficient protein dbfp7 adheres to the surface remains unclear. Using all atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling, we studied the mussel foot protein dbfp7, both short sequence-motif peptides and the intact N-terminal fragment across multiple conformers and orientations using rutile titanium oxide surface (110). Individual residues bind only weakly (at or below thermal energy) to the surface and binding did not strengthen with peptide length. Nonetheless, the intact protein fragment adheres irreversibly to the surface, engaging with multiple different interfaces rather than a single binding site. Aromatic residues were enriched at the interface when exposed to the surface but were not required, as an aromatic-poor face also binds equally well. These findings suggest that dbfp7 adheres to the surface through the collective action of many weak, non-specific contacts, providing a mechanism for robust adhesion in the absence of catechol chemistry.

title: Temperature-induced Changes to the Nucleation Mechanism of MOF-5-inspired Crystals through the Lens of Multiscale Simulation
abstract: A comprehensive map of metal-organic framework (MOF) formation mechanisms is crucial to facilitate the experimental realization and/or synthesis optimization of computer-generated MOFs. Experiments to gain this knowledge face challenges with the time and length scales of the crucial MOF nucleation stage and the interplay of a multitude of synthesis-relevant factors. In response to this challenge, this work uses molecular simulation to isolate the effect of temperature, one of the most common processing conditions used to optimize MOF solvothermal synthesis, on the nucleation mechanism of porous, cubic crystals representative of the prototypical material MOF-5. The simulation framework used herein is multiscale, culminating with coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations enhanced with Hamiltonian replica exchange (HREX), enabling the construction of free energy surfaces (FESs) and minimum free energy pathway (MFEP) analysis. This analysis suggests that MOF-5 nucleation in DMF follows a non-classical, multistage nucleation pathway at the studied temperatures (i.e., 300 K, 413 K, and 500 K), where metastable amorphous nuclei form prominently before annealing into ordered cubic nuclei, following a multibarrier free energy pathway. Critically, consistent with the well-established solvothermal synthesis of MOF-5 in DMF at ~ 413 K, our analysis identifies this temperature as more kinetically favorable than 300 K and 500 K. Briefly, it exhibits the smoothest free energy landscape from dense liquid to nucleus formation, the highest equilibrium population of the cubic nucleus, and the fastest rate for nucleus formation. These factors collectively rationalize why this temperature range may be favored in practice. Similarities and differences in the sequence of events leading to formation of large, ordered nuclei across the studied temperatures are discussed as well.

title: Sulfated Prism[6]arene Binds One Guest Internally and One Guest Externally
abstract: We report the synthesis of sulfated prism[6]arene (Pr[6]AS) by reaction of (HO)12Pr[6] with SO3•pyridine in 35% yield. Pr[6]AS has very good solubility in water (>30 mM) and does not undergo self-association according to 1H NMR dilution experiments. Qualitative 1H NMR investigations show that guest resonances shift dramatically upfield and become significantly broadened upon complexation with Pr[6]AS. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments show that Pr[6]AS forms ternary complexes (Pr[6]AS•guest2) with hydrophobic ammonium ions in phosphate buffered saline with b-values (Ka1 x Ka2) values up to 6.84 x 1013 M-2. Molecular dynamics simulations show that Pr[6]AS firmly binds one Me4Bipip guest within its cavity and a second Me4Bipip guest on the convex region of Pr[6]AS in close proximity to the externally directed sulfate substituents. Uncomplexed Pr[6]AS holds 7.6 ± 1.9 H2O and one Na+ ion within its cavity. Formation of the 1:1 and 1:2 Pr[6]AS-Me4Bipip complexes results in expulsion of the Na+ ion and approximately five of the solvating H2O molecules. Intriguingly, the combination of larger naphthalene walls and sulfate ionic groups that are conformationally restricted creates a secondary guest binding site on the exterior of Pr[6]AS which suggests a route toward design of high molecularity complexes.

title: Population-Specific H-Antigen Chain-Type Variation and Its Potential Impact on Enzymatic Universal-Blood Conversion: A Computational Pilot Study
abstract: Enzymatic conversion of donor blood to universal type O ("ECO blood") is an active area of transfusion medicine research, with recently discovered bacterial enzymes capable of removing canonical and structurally extended ABO blood-group antigens. Whether human genetic variation affecting antigen chaintype distribution influences the efficiency of these conversion enzymes has not previously been examined. Using FucOB, a structurally characterized alpha-1,2-fucosidase, as a test case, we combined published mutagenesis data with molecular docking to compare its interaction with two physiologically dominant chain-type variants of the H blood-group antigen (type I and type II), whose relative abundance on red blood cells is genetically determined by FUT2 secretor status. We find a reproducible docking asymmetry tighter, more consistent binding to H type I than to H type II - that holds under two independent scoring methods. Combining this finding with published Indian FUT2 non-secretor phenotype frequencies (20-33%, varying by region), we estimate that a substantial minority of the Indian population may experience reduced FucOB conversion efficiency due tolacking H type Ichainsentirely.Thisisapreliminary computational finding requiring experimental validation; we report it, together with full methodological transparency and an explicit accounting of AI-assisted contributions, to invite expert scrutiny before further investment.

title: Rescuable Stagnation: A Diagnostic for Benchmark Suitability in LLM-Guided Materials Optimization
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly incorporated into closed-loop materials optimization, yet existing benchmarks provide little controlled evidence of what they contribute once Bayesian optimization stalls. We introduce a benchmark qualification criterion for rescue experiments—which we term rescuable stagnation—for determining, before the optimization comparison is run, whether a benchmark stalls while meaningful improvement remains available. Benchmarks that fail this test make it difficult to distinguish ineffective rescue strategies from saturated or non-stalling optimization. Qualifying a benchmark in advance therefore reduces the risk that null results reflect benchmark design rather than the method under evaluation. We demonstrate the approach on a benchmark constructed from Materials Project shear-modulus data, on which LLM-guided rescue gives no statistically significant improvement over heuristic injection—including a heuristic control provided with the same search information. The LLM nonetheless steers the search toward chemically distinct, high-modulus regions that conventional heuristics do not reach. This exploration behavior reproduces across two model capability levels and does not depend on the coherence of the model’s rationales, though it carries a substantially higher per-proposal cost. The LLM’s distinctive contribution on this benchmark is therefore in where it places exploration rather than in the optimization outcome it achieves, though this distinctiveness did not translate into a measurable advantage under the budget tested. More broadly, conclusions about LLM-guided discovery hinge on benchmark suitability—which qualifying the benchmark makes testable before experiments begin.

title: Conditional GraphGANFed: Optimizing Graph-Structured Molecule Generation in Federated Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have garnered considerable attention in molecular discovery for their ability to generate novel and high-quality molecules. To efficiently train a GAN model while preserving data privacy, GraphGANFed has been proposed to incorporate federated learning and graph convolutional networks into GAN. Yet, GraphGANFed cannot produce synthetic molecules that only optimize a user-defined metric(s) to facilitate the new drug discovery process. To address this issue, we introduce a novel extension to GraphGANFed, namely conditional GraphGANFed (cGraphGANFed), by incorporating the critic network to assess generated molecules using user-defined metric(s). The evaluation results from both the critic network and discriminator are integrated into the loss function of the generator, guiding it to generate novel molecules that maintain similar chemical properties to real ones while optimizing user-defined metrics. Extensive simulations are conducted in two scenarios. First, cGraphGANFed endeavors to optimize all seven commonly used metrics, and the results show that cGraphGANFed significantly outperforms GraphGANFed in Validity and LogP, with a slight advantage in QED, across different settings. Second, cGraphGANFed focuses solely on optimizing QED, and the results show that the synthetic molecules produced by cGraphGANFed can achieve more than 10% improvement in QED than GraphGANFed. Also, the results demonstrate cGraphGANFed has enhanced resilience against mode collapses and performance reduction caused by non-IID data.

title: Explain and Go Beyond with Surfacia: A Surface-Descriptor based Workflow for Interpretable Molecular Machine Learning
abstract: Machine-learning models are widely used in chemistry, yet black-box predictions are often difficult to translate into chemically actionable descriptor-response rules or candidate-prioritization decisions. We present Surfacia, an automated workflow that transforms molecular structures and target values into wavefunction-derived surface descriptors, compact interpretable models, SHAP-based chemical interpretation, and visualization. The Surfacia descriptor system contains two complementary components: whole-molecule physical descriptors, which summarize geometry, orbital properties, and statistics of real-space molecular-surface functions, including electrostatic potential (ESP), average local ionization energy (ALIE), and local electron attachment energy (LEAE); and multi-scale quantitative surface analysis (MQSA) descriptors, which reorganize these surface properties around chemically meaningful units. We evaluated Surfacia on three case studies: sulfur-containing modifiers in carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR), a homologous organocatalyst series, and the Estimated SOLubility (ESOL) benchmark. The Results and Discussion are organized in two layers. First, compact selected Surfacia models are interpreted as chemically readable regression models. Second, a separate frontier-conditioned acquisition analysis asks whether the same sparse descriptor-SHAP landscape can support high-value candidate prioritization under a limited experimental budget. This second layer formalizes the chemist's go-beyond question as a sequential discovery problem: given only the current labeled set and a hidden frontier candidate pool, which acquisition rule can reach the true top-1 candidate with the lowest experimental cost? The comparison shows that descriptor-space novelty is the most stable region-entry signal, while SHAP-derived landscape information provides an interpretable way to order candidates within or around those novel regions. Thus, Surfacia connects mechanistically legible descriptor-response interpretation with a practical framework for discovery-oriented candidate selection, without requiring the SHAP-cliff variant to be universally superior to all novelty or diversity baselines.

title: Polymer-Linked Nanoparticle Networks Running on Heat Can Act as Computing Devices
abstract: Developing physical neural network (PNN) hardwares is important to next generation artificial intelligence systems. Phononic devices-using heat current to encode and process information-is one of the solutions to neuromorphic computing. In this work, we back map an artificial neural network (ANN) into a PNN simulation model using polymer networked nanoparticles (PNNPs). Our atomistic simulation results demonstrate that the polymer linked nanoparticle networks can potentially realize information processing using heat current. Using high-throughput molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the trust region Bayesian optimization (TuRBO) methods, we tune the plasticity of polymer linkers and the temperatures of nanoparticles to optimize the performance of the PNNP machines, which is similar to tune the weights and bias in ANNs. After 5 rounds of high-throughput MD simulations, we show that the PNNP machines have improved in performance. We also use a testing data set to verify the heat flow outputs from the top 5 PNNP machines in each round.

title: PathoMIC: A Benchmark for Cross-Species Antimicrobial Peptide Activity Prediction
abstract: With activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens and mechanisms distinct from conventional antibiotics, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising approach to combating antibiotic-resistant infections. However, their potency varies substantially across pathogen species, making accurate prediction of the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) for specific peptide-pathogen pairs essential for prioritizing candidates before costly experimental validation. Existing predictors are trained mainly on a few well-represented pathogens and rarely exploit biological relationships across species, limiting their generalization to low-resource and unseen pathogens. We introduce PathoMIC, the largest and most pathogen-diverse unified dataset for quantitative antimicrobial peptide activity prediction, containing 74,751 experimentally reported MIC measurements across 424 pathogen species. PathoMIC integrates peptide sequences, standardized MIC values, pathogen descriptions, and taxonomic relationships to facilitate knowledge transfer across related species. We establish few-shot and zero-shot cross-species evaluation protocols and develop a knowledge-enhanced framework that leverages pathogen descriptions and taxonomy. The framework yields substantial improvements for low-resource species with limited supervision, while gains for entirely unseen species remain modest, highlighting the difficulty of zero-shot cross-species MIC prediction. PathoMIC provides a standardized foundation for cross-species activity modeling and pathogen-specific virtual screening. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PathoMIC-546D/.

title: SmartReact: An Open-Source Python Package for Scalable Forward Synthesis Enumeration Built on Interpretable SMARTS Templates
abstract: Predicting which products can be made from a set of building blocks underpins library design, analogue generation, and synthesis-constrained generative modelling. Reaction templates encoded as SMARTS patterns are the standard tool for this forward synthesis enumeration task. However, existing approaches force a trade-off between chemical coverage, specificity, and the computational cost of applying large template sets at scale. We present SmartReact, an open-source Python library whose template set inverts that trade-off, because the construction that produces the specificity is the same construction that makes the templates cheap to eliminate. Its templates are combinatorial expansions over SMARTS-RX, a fixed hierarchical functional group ontology of 406 patterns, so the library exposes only a few hundred distinct reactant-side patterns no matter how many templates it holds, and one classification per molecule resolves thousands of templates at once. Every prediction of SmartReact is traceable to a named reaction and an explicit set of functional group requirements, making results directly interpretable by chemists and straightforward to audit. New reaction types can be incorporated by specifying a SMARTS pattern and its functional group requirements, making the library easy to extend. A case study enumerating 536,171 unique products from 1,000 building blocks in 15.7 s demonstrates real-world utility at scale. Scientific Contribution: SmartReact contributes a large, expert-refined SMARTS reaction template library together with an open-source Python package designed to use it efficiently. The library's 9,770 templates spanning 37 medicinal chemistry reaction types are generated by combinatorial expansion over the SMARTS-RX functional group ontology, which gives them a chemical specificity and non-redundancy that auto-extracted libraries lack and, at the same time, a bounded reactant-side pattern space that makes them cheap to pre-filter.

title: FragFlow: depth-resolved cosolvent mapping recovers cryptic and allosteric sites inside lipid bilayers
abstract: Cosolvent molecular dynamics maps druggable hotspots by seeding small organic probes into a simulation, accumulating their density, and converting density to free energy against a single scalar bulk reference. That reference is what has kept the method from scoring a site inside the membrane: probes have been mapped there, but against a background that does not know how deep it is. A hydrophobic probe partitions into the acyl core, so referenced to bulk water the bilayer itself is a hotspot: benzene’s transfer free energy into a protein-free POPC core is −3.34 kcal mol−1, and the core sits at 48-146× bulk-water probe density (Table S1) before any protein is present. We replace the scalar reference with a depth-resolved one. Reduced membrane depth ζ = 2·d/⟨DPP⟩ is measured per frame, and every voxel is scored against the far-field probe density at its own depth (Algorithm S1), taken from the same simulation box. On three proteins spanning three architectures (a mitochondrial carrier, a class-A G-protein-coupled receptor, and a twopore-domain potassium channel) the false-positive rate of a frozen detection rule in non-site acyl-core voxels falls from 43.5-63.6 % to 0.03-0.44 % (Table S2), measured out-of-sample on identical voxels with only the reference term exchanged. The gain is in specificity and it is a deliberate trade, quantified on both sides: discrimination between the scored site and non-site core voxels rises from 1.72×, 1.74× and 0.65× to 1843×, 104× and 15.7×, the first of these measured against a predicted candidate and the other two against experimentally validated sites, and a scalar value below unity means that reference fires more often on non-sites than on sites. The price is that firing at the validated sites falls from 75.0 %, 85.7 % and 41.4 % to 50.0 %, 7.1 % and 6.9 % at the same fixed threshold. We regard that as the correct trade: a method that fires on the whole bilayer has no use for the sensitivity it appears to retain: the first of these against a predicted candidate rather than a validated site, the other two against experimentally validated ones; the scalar value below unity means that reference fires more often on non-sites than on sites. FragFlow localizes a co-crystallized antagonist site without being given its position (98 % of the detected region lies within 5 Å of the ligand) and declines the same receptor’s orthosteric pocket; we show that this recovery rests on the geometry, hydration, lining and occupancy channels and not on the fragment score, which ranks a neighboring non-site lobe above the true site. It also identifies a transient hydrophobic cavity on the carrier at ζ = −0.77. We further show that the reference’s shape is reproducible to 0.039 kcal mol−1 between replicates while its level scatters by 0.411, that binding-site residence resolves into components spanning two orders of magnitude that no mean describes, and that a probe cannot report on a site it does not enter.

title: Cross-Temperature Defect Identification in Atomistic Simulations via Multi-Level Domain Alignment
abstract: Identifying atomic defects at elevated temperature is difficult because thermal fluctuations blur the local symmetry that both geometric heuristics and supervised classifiers rely on: trustworthy labels exist in low-temperature reference configurations, while the high-temperature regime where robust analysis matters most is effectively unlabeled. We cast this as a cross-temperature domain-shift problem and align the two domains at three levels: an equivariant denoiser at the input level, cross-temperature contrastive learning at the representation level, and a morphology-aware regularizer that steers predictions toward the compact geometry of physical defect structures. Because no atom-wise truth exists at temperature, we further introduce a label-free evaluation suite that scores predicted defect structures along five spatial and physics-based axes, enabling model assessment and selection without high-temperature labels. Near the melting point, the framework identifies vacancies and self-interstitial atoms across face-centered-cubic, body-centered-cubic, and hexagonal-close-packed iron systems with every interstitial localized and zero false detections in every vacancy system against Wigner-Seitz ground truth, with no high-temperature labels used in training. It sustains this fidelity on a million-atom, 2.5 ns trajectory, resolving single vacancy hops and complete Frenkel-pair recombination, and captures grain-boundary phase transformations in aluminum bicrystals, distinguishing two nucleation modes. Multi-level domain alignment thus offers a practical, label-efficient route to temperature-robust structural analysis of large-scale molecular dynamics.

title: Development of the 12-6-4-3B Model: Incorporating Nonadditive Three-Body Interactions into Metal Ion Simulations
abstract: Metal ions play fundamental roles in diverse biological and materials systems, yet accurately simulating them with force field models remains challenging due to pronounced polarization and charge transfer effects, which are intrinsically many-body in character. For example, Zn2+ serves as an essential co-factor in many important proteins. It can adopt coordination numbers of 4, 5, and 6 in aqueous phase and metalloenzymes, and capturing both the equilibrium among these states and the kinetic barriers connecting them remains difficult. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA) offers a lens into distinct energy components, providing deeper insight into contributions of different physical origin. By combining SobEDA with many-body expansion (MBE) framework, we systematically investigated the many-body EDA components for the [Zn(H2O)n]2+ (n = 2 − 6) clusters. Our results show the orbital term—representing polarization and charge transfer—dominates the three-body and higher-order contributions. Furthermore, many-body interactions in metal ion complexes converge considerably more slowly than in pure water: the many-body expansion for Zn2+ in aqueous solution is oscillatory, with successive terms alternating in sign and decaying slowly, such that four-body and higher-order contributions remain non-negligible. To examine how the water–ion–water three-body term depends on molecular geometry, we systematically scanned this trimer system by varying the ion–water distance and the water–ion–water angle. Using EDA throughout the scan and reasoning from the physical origins of each term, we proposed and parameterized three-body terms, yielding the 12-6-4-3B model, which explicitly incorporates three-body effects into a classical force field. Conventional 12-6 and 12-6-4 potentials, though widely used for metal ions in molecular dynamics simulations, are effectively pairwise and capture many-body effects only implicitly, which cannot simultaneously reproduce the water exchange mechanism and energetics of Zn2+. By contrast, after adjusting the C4 term, the 12-6-4-3B model correctly reproduces both the water exchange mechanism and the associated free energy barrier, demonstrating the benefit of explicitly incorporating three-body terms in metal ion force fields.

title: Total Synthesis: Backbone of Organic Chemistry, a Discipline in Decline?
abstract: Total synthesis has long been regarded as the intellectual backbone of organic chemistry, driving reaction discovery, stereoselective methodology, and molecular design. Yet its place within the contemporary discipline is actively debated, largely on the basis of editorial opinion rather than evidence. In this Perspective we bring quantitative data to that debate. We examined the annual share of articles carrying the phrase “total synthesis” in their titles across four leading journals—Angewandte Chemie International Edition, Journal of Organic Chemistry, Organic Letters, and Tetrahedron Letters—from 1959 to 2025. The share rose through the late twentieth century to a peak of about 4.79% in 2009, then fell to 1.85% by 2025, a relative decline of roughly 61%. Structural-break analysis places a consistent inflection near 2020, and an AIC-selected ARIMA(0,1,0) model with drift projects continued decline to about 1.40% by 2030. Crucially, the fall is relative rather than absolute: the annual number of total syntheses has held broadly steady while overall journal output has expanded dramatically. We argue that total synthesis is not disappearing but being diluted and redefined, and we outline how researchers, editors, and funding agencies might sustain it as a driver of innovation.

title: Divergent CRAM formation and persistence across freshwater and marine environments revealed by AI-expanded MS/MS libraries
abstract: Carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM) are a major refractory component of marine dissolved organic matter (DOM), yet their isomeric structures and formation chemistry remain sparsely represented in public MS/MS libraries. We trained a Property Conditioned Transformer Variant Autoencoder (VAE) —Enhanced Hierarchical GAT with Ring Chain Encoder, 64-dimensional 40 latent code, 17D property head on z, and a six-layer Transformer SELFIES decoder—on a curated CRAM-focused set (n = 5,842) and compiled an environmentally screened in silico library of 5.04 million structures. On a 10,000-molecule audit sample, 57.6% of generated molecules satisfied all four strict CRAM criteria, corresponding to enrichment ratio = 210.3 [128.9, 343.2], 95% CI, relative to training occupancy (16/5,842). Evaluated on 476,647 spectra from 98 sources spanning open-ocean, deep-sea, coastal, coral-reef, and riverine DOM, the library expanded CRAM-region formula coverage from 4,296 to 7,069 unique formulas and isomer candidates from 5,401 to 13,519. Within TRFU CRAM-compositional features (O/C 0.3–0.6, H/C 0.7–1.5; n = 18,513), explained peak ratio (EPR) rose from 31.8% under PubChem-only top hits to 38.0% under max-over-union retrieval across libraries (+6.2 percentage points), with CRAM-library hits alone reaching 40.4%. Mass-difference networks from the same 98 sources were oxidation-rich across environments, with riverine networks showing elevated alkylation and a stronger alkylation-to-hydrolysis Markov contribution. NPClassifier pathway mixes place alkaloid-associated labels among the largest marine CRAM-node classes alongside terpenoids and shikimates, with riverine polyketide-associated labels elevated; pooled non-CRAM to CRAM formation edges further show alkaloid-like labels declining and terpenoid-like labels rising. Microbial-molecular docking confirmed that network CRAM ligands are sterically compatible with diverse bacterial enzymes (global mean ΔG = −6.45 kcal mol-1; 1,324 ligands / 846 pairs). Together, property-conditioned generative expansion measurably strengthens environmental MS/MS annotation and enables source-resolved, annotation-supported pathway 59 comparisons beyond formula-level description.

title: InP Quantum Dots, from Atomistic Reconstruction to Opto-Electronic Properties
abstract: The molecular orbitals of semiconductor nanocrystals or quantum dots (QDs) strongly depend on the size, shape and surface termination of the crystallite. However, directly relating the energy level structure to an atomically precise QD geometry has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we reconstruct the geometry of InP QDs from quantitative scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) images by means of atom counting and molecular dynamics simulations. We identify six structural features, which include In-terminated (111) and (100) facets, a stacking fault, and P-terminated (−111) facets. According to density functional theory (DFT) calculations, this surface termination gives rise to delocalized conduction-band orbitals, and a broad band of occupied surface-localized orbitals above the InP bulk valence-band edge. While showing no measurable photoluminescence, femtosecond pulsed excitation leads to a welldefined band-edge bleach, even when using below-band gap pump light, that persists for several nanoseconds. We argue that this observation agrees with the computational prediction of well-defined conduction-band orbitals and occupied, surface-localized orbitals. This demonstrated interplay between the experimentally verified geometry and energy level structure creates a new paradigm for analyzing surface geometry / electronic structure relations in QDs.

title: Insights into Lithium Diffusion in Crystalline and Amorphous Solid Electrolytes with Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Amorphization is a widely used approach to tune the ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes, but its effect in different anion chemistries remains poorly understood. In this work, we employ molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to quantify the effects of amorphization on Li-ion transport in lithium solid electrolytes from three anion chemistries: Li3YCl6 (LYC), Li0.33La0.56TiO3 (LLTO) and Li7P3S11 (LPS). With amorphization, it is observed that the ionic conductivity increases for LYC, decreases for LLTO and remains relatively unchanged for LPS, in agreement with previous experiments. Coordination analysis at 300K reveals that these ionic conductivity changes can be correlated with amorphization-induced changes in Li-anion coordination environments; decreases in coordination increase ionic conductivity and vice versa. These different responses show that the effect of amorphization on Li-ion diffusion behavior is not universal and is governed by specific anion coordination motifs.

title: Decoding Resonance and Nonresonance Raman Spectra of Biological Systems using Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Raman spectroscopy has been widely employed for advancing our understanding of biological systems, such as determining protein secondary structures, tracing chemical reactions, and studying therapeutically relevant biological species. To decode the complicated and convoluted Raman spectra into meaningful atomistic level information, peak assignment is indispensable. Herein, we proposed a unique method that computes the Raman spectra and assigns the complex spectra to Raman fingerprints based on the bond polarizability model. Using this method, we computed the resonance and nonresonance Raman spectra of real biological systems, such as protein and B-DNA, and successfully assigned each peak to atomic groups.

title: Text Embedding-Assisted Prediction of Corrosion Inhibition Efficiency Using Machine Learning under Small-Sample Conditions
abstract: Machine learning has been increasingly applied to corrosion prediction, but limited experimental data remain a challenge for small-sample prediction. This study investigates how text embedding can be used as a molecular representation for predicting the corrosion inhibition efficiency of organic inhibitors for ZE41 magnesium alloy. An experimental dataset containing 75 inhibitors was used, with 60 samples for training and 15 samples for testing. Conventional molecular descriptors were combined with text embeddings generated using ChemBERTa and Qwen-text-embedding-v4, and five feature construction strategies were compared to examine the effects of embedding dimensionality and feature integration. Direct incorporation of high-dimensional ChemBERTa embeddings provided limited improvement, whereas dimensionality reduction improved the prediction performance. A selective hybrid strategy was further investigated, in which selected descriptors were incorporated into the text embedding while other descriptors were retained in their original numerical form. This strategy achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.61 and a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.79, compared to those of 0.12 and 0.43, respectively, for the conventional descriptor-based representation. The results suggest that text embedding may be more useful as a complementary representation to conventional molecular descriptors than as a direct replacement, when experimental data are limited.

title: Electrostatic Pre-solvation Enables Selectivity in Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
abstract: Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σcomplex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H s-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is enabled by electrostatic pre-solvation, which orients the acetonitrile methyl groups toward the metal center prior to CO dissociation. Our results point to a general strategy to direct selectivity in C–H activation by controlling coordination through pre-solvation.
